result:
Before I write this up, there's one more choice about how it gets built. The museum's site is a static site on Netlify, so it can't accept uploads on its own. Where the guide lives and how a volunteer's recording reaches it shapes most of the design.

**(1) Guide pages on your existing site, recordings stored in the site's code.** Each exhibit gets a page like `harbourmuseum.org/guide/anchor-chain`, and the code beside the exhibit opens it. Visitors need no app. Volunteers use a simple editing screen added to the site. Each upload is saved into the site's files, cleaned up, and published with the next site update.
- Trade-off: it's the fewest new parts.
- But 120 recordings, plus ten new stories a year in two languages, make the site's files heavy.
- Each new recording also waits for a full site update before visitors hear it.

**(2) Guide pages on your existing site, recordings stored separately.** Visitors get the same pages and the same codes. Volunteers use a small password-protected upload page. Each recording goes to file storage alongside the site, gets cleaned up as it arrives, and is live within a minute or so.
- Trade-off: one more piece to look after, the storage, which is a few pounds a month at most at your size.
- The site itself stays light.

**(3) An off-the-shelf audio-guide service.** You pay a subscription and get their app or player and their upload tool.
- Trade-off: almost nothing to build.
- But it costs more every year, your Welsh support depends on what they offer, and the clean-up step is theirs to do or not.

I recommend **(2)**. It keeps the guide part of your own site, adds recordings without anyone technical, and the clean-up you chose fits naturally into the upload step.

This is a project-sized piece of work. Once you pick, I'll write the full design as a document in the repository. A reviewer will read it first, and I may come back once with a few questions before handing it over.

Which way do you want to go?
